`_get_order_from_query_object` accepts a user-supplied adhoc orderby element (`{"sqlExpression": ...}`) and wraps its raw `sqlExpression` into an `AdhocExpression(definition=...)` with no validation. Unlike the column/dimension paths in the same file — which only accept names present in the semantic view's `all_dimensions`/`all_metrics` allowlists — the orderby adhoc branch forwards arbitrary SQL text verbatim. Per the matcher guidance, attacker-authorable SQL fragments should pass `validate_adhoc_subquery` / `validate_stored_expression` (single-statement, no set-ops, no disallowed subqueries) before being embedded. The resulting `AdhocExpression` is handed to the semantic-layer driver (`query_object.datasource.implementation`) for execution; if a driver renders `definition` into warehouse SQL, this could allow SQL injection / reading beyond the semantic view's exposed columns. No in-repo driver consumes `AdhocExpression`, so the concrete SQL sink is in external/pluggable driver code and could not be confirmed here.

##### Attack Path

```
chart-data request orderby [{sqlExpression: "..."}, ...] --ValidatedQueryObject.orderby--> _get_order_from_query_object --unvalidated AdhocExpression(definition=sqlExpression)--> SemanticQuery.order --> driver.implementation renders SQL (out-of-repo) --> potential SQLi / column-restriction bypass
```

The column and dimension branches enforce allowlists, but the `isinstance(element, dict)` orderby branch copies `element['sqlExpression']` directly into `AdhocExpression.definition`. `SemanticQuery` objects are then passed to the datasource's `implementation` driver. Whether raw embedding occurs depends on the driver; standard Superset applies `validate_adhoc_subquery` to adhoc expressions before literal embedding, and that validation is absent on this path.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker has datasource access to a semantic view and can call the chart-data query API against it with a crafted `orderby` adhoc expression.
- A semantic-layer driver implementation renders `AdhocExpression.definition` into executed warehouse SQL (unverified — no such driver exists in this repository).

{"category": "open-redirect", "code_owners": ["PRATHAMESH HUKKERI <prathamhukkeri04@gmail.com>", "Mike Bridge <michael.bridge@preset.io>"], "code_scan_run_id": "csrun-7f80d40c5f5546f0b1d3b9d6690cd01a", "created_at": 1788537731, "description": "##### Overview

The deprecated `Superset.explore` POST handler redirects the browser to `datasource.default_endpoint` verbatim when no `viz_type` is present in the form data. `default_endpoint` is a free-form string column that is writable through the dataset create/update REST API (`DatasetPostSchema` / `DatasetPutSchema`) with no URL/host validation on write and no `is_safe_url`-style check before the redirect. A user with dataset-edit capability can therefore store an absolute external URL (e.g. `https://evil.example`) that is later served as a 302 `Location` to any user who opens that dataset in the legacy explore view, yielding a stored open redirect usable for phishing.

##### Attack Path

```
Alpha/dataset-owner sets dataset.default_endpoint = "https://evil.example" via PUT /api/v1/dataset/<id>
   --stored unvalidated--> connectors.sqla.models.SqlaTable.default_endpoint
   --victim POSTs /superset/explore/ for that dataset with no viz_type-->
   redirect(datasource.default_endpoint) --302 Location--> https://evil.example
```

The dataset schema accepts `default_endpoint` as an arbitrary string (no validator). At explore time the code checks only `not viz_type and datasource and datasource.default_endpoint` and then calls Flask `redirect()` on the raw value, so an absolute off-site URL is emitted as the redirect target. `security_manager.raise_for_access(datasource=datasource)` gates *reading* the datasource but does not constrain the redirect destination.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker holds a role with dataset write capability (Alpha, or a dataset owner) to set `default_endpoint`; Gamma cannot normally create/edit datasets.
- Victim has read access to that dataset and reaches the deprecated `/superset/explore/` **POST** path (GET returns before line 253). Because the trigger is a POST, it is CSRF-protected, so the victim must submit the request themselves rather than following an attacker link — this materially weakens the classic GET-link phishing vector.
- The legacy explore view (`@deprecated`) is still enabled.", "finding_id": "sfind-516a06a67e304b2089409aeb1d137df5", "note": "Deprecated Superset.explore POST (views/core.py:251-253) redirects to dataset.default_endpoint verbatim; default_endpoint is writable via dataset create/update REST API with no URL validation, yielding a stored open redirect. Heavily mitigated: requires dataset-write (Alpha/owner) to plant, the trigger is a CSRF-protected POST so the victim must self-submit (not a click-through link), and the legacy @deprecated explore view must still be enabled. Presto/Trino table-metadata introspection builds raw SQL by interpolating the caller-supplied `schema` and `table` names directly into query strings without quoting or escaping. `PrestoEngineSpec.get_create_view()` builds `SHOW CREATE VIEW {schema}.{table}` and `_partition_query()` builds `SELECT * FROM {schema}."{table}$partitions"` / `SHOW PARTITIONS FROM {schema}.{table}`. These names originate from the `name`/`schema` query-string parameters of the `/api/v1/database/<pk>/table_metadata/extra/` (and deprecated `/table_extra/`) endpoint. Because `raise_for_access(database, table)` grants access to *any* table name when the caller has `schema_access` on the supplied schema (or `database_access`), a user who holds only schema-level access — not the `sql_lab` capability — can inject arbitrary text into the identifier portion of an introspection statement executed against the connection. This is an identifier-quoting defect: sibling paths in the same file (`_show_columns` via `quote_table`, and the SQLAlchemy inspector) correctly quote identifiers, so the intended pattern is being violated here.

##### Attack Path

```
GET /api/v1/database/<pk>/table_metadata/extra/?name=<injection>&schema=<schema-user-can-access>
  --request args--> Table(name, schema) --raise_for_access(schema_access match) passes-->
  PrestoEngineSpec.get_extra_table_metadata --> get_create_view(database, schema, table)
  --f-string--> "SHOW CREATE VIEW {schema}.{table}" --cls.execute(cursor, sql)--> raw SQL on Presto connection
```

The `table_extra_metadata` handler loads `name`/`schema`/`catalog` from `request.args` via `QualifiedTableSchema` (string validation only) and calls `raise_for_access(database=database, table=table)`. In `SecurityManager.raise_for_access`, the `database and table` branch returns access as granted if `can_access_database` is true, or if the caller has `schema_access` on the supplied `schema` (the per-table dataset match is skipped because `force_dataset_match` defaults to False on this path). The attacker-controlled `table` string is then passed unquoted into `get_create_view`, which interpolates it into `SHOW CREATE VIEW {schema}.{table}` and executes it on the raw connection. `get_create_view` is called unconditionally by `get_extra_table_metadata`, so it is always reached. Real-world impact is constrained: Presto/Trino DBAPI does not permit stacking multiple statements in one `execute`, and `SHOW CREATE VIEW` does not accept sub-selects or `UNION`, so an attacker cannot straightforwardly turn this into arbitrary data exfiltration. The higher-impact `_partition_query` `SELECT ... $partitions` path is only reached when `get_indexes(table)` returns indexes, and `get_indexes` uses the SQLAlchemy inspector (which quotes/parameterizes the literal name), so an injection payload as the table name resolves to no such table and the partition query is not built. The residual issue is therefore an unquoted-identifier injection with limited demonstrated escalation, filed for defense-in-depth and for aggregation with any sibling sink that could make the injected name reach an executable statement.

##### Preconditions

- Target database is a Presto or Trino connection (this engine spec).
- Attacker holds a Superset account with `schema_access` on at least one schema of that database (or broader `database_access`) but not the `sql_lab` capability — i.e. they are entitled to browse metadata for that schema but not to run arbitrary SQL. This is the `schema_access` / `database_access` row of the SECURITY.md capability matrix; the escalation target is the `sql_lab` (arbitrary SQL execution) capability.
- Attacker calls `/api/v1/database/<pk>/table_metadata/extra/` (or the deprecated `/table_extra/<table>/<schema>/`) with a crafted `name` value, using a `schema` they can access so the access check passes.", "finding_id": "sfind-e448f21b7460405a9277024816ee8f52", "note": "Triage: P2 (defense-in-depth). Exploitability difficult / limited escalation: requires a Presto/Trino connection + attacker holding schema_access on a schema of that db. When neither the raw expression nor the synthetic `SELECT <expr>` form can be parsed by sqlglot in either the engine dialect or the permissive `base` dialect, the function logs a warning and returns the expression unvalidated. Unlike the column/dimension paths in the same file — which only accept names present in the semantic view's `all_dimensions`/`all_metrics` allowlists — the orderby adhoc branch forwards arbitrary SQL text verbatim. Per the matcher guidance, attacker-authorable SQL fragments should pass `validate_adhoc_subquery` / `validate_stored_expression` (single-statement, no set-ops, no disallowed subqueries) before being embedded. The column and dimension branches enforce allowlists, but the `isinstance(element, dict)` orderby branch copies `element['sqlExpression']` directly into `AdhocExpression.definition`. `SemanticQuery` objects are then passed to the datasource's `implementation` driver. Unlike the sibling `charts` and `dashboards` lists in the same response — which are each filtered with per-object `security_manager.can_access_*` checks — the `sqllab_tab_states` list is returned unfiltered. `DatabaseDAO.get_related_objects` selects every `TabState` row for the database regardless of its owning `user_id`, so a user leaks other users' SQL Lab tab labels, ids and active flags. The explore GET endpoint (`GET /api/v1/explore/`, `GetExploreCommand.run`) authorizes access using the chart (`slc`) when a `slice_id` resolves to a chart the caller can read, but the datasource whose full definition it returns is taken from the request-controlled `form_data["datasource"]`. Because the caller controls `form_data` and can point it at any dataset id, a low-privilege authenticated user who can read even a single chart can retrieve the full definition of any dataset in the system — its virtual-dataset SQL, column definitions, metric SQL expressions, physical `table_name`/`schema`/`catalog`, `select_star`, `params`, `perm`, and database name/backend — for datasets they are not granted. This violates the object-level access control that normally gates datasets.

##### Attack Path

```
Gamma user (owns/can read >=1 chart) --GET /api/v1/explore/?slice_id=<accessible chart>&form_data={"datasource":"<victim_dataset_id>__table","slice_id":<accessible chart>}--> get_form_data (slc = accessible chart, passes can_access_chart) --slice_form_data.update(form_data) overrides datasource--> get_datasource_info returns victim_dataset_id --> datasource = victim dataset --> `if slc: raise_for_access(chart=slc)` checks ONLY the accessible chart, NOT victim dataset --> datasource.data returns victim dataset definition (sql, columns, metrics, schema) --leads to--> cross-boundary dataset definition disclosure
```

In `get_form_data` (superset/views/utils.py), when `slice_id` resolves to a chart the caller can read, the stored chart form data is merged with the request form data via `slice_form_data.update(form_data)`, so an attacker-supplied `datasource` key overrides the chart's own datasource. Presto/Trino table-metadata introspection builds raw SQL by interpolating the caller-supplied `schema` and `table` names directly into query strings without quoting or escaping. `PrestoEngineSpec.get_create_view()` builds `SHOW CREATE VIEW {schema}.{table}` and `_partition_query()` builds `SELECT * FROM {schema}."{table}$partitions"` / `SHOW PARTITIONS FROM {schema}.{table}`. These names originate from the `name`/`schema` query-string parameters of the `/api/v1/database/<pk>/table_metadata/extra/` (and deprecated `/table_extra/`) endpoint. Because `raise_for_access(database, table)` grants access to *any* table name when the caller has `schema_access` on the supplied schema (or `database_access`), a user who holds only schema-level access — not the `sql_lab` capability — can inject arbitrary text into the identifier portion of an introspection statement executed against the connection. This is an identifier-quoting defect: sibling paths in the same file (`_show_columns` via `quote_table`, and the SQLAlchemy inspector) correctly quote identifiers, so the intended pattern is being violated here.

##### Attack Path

```
GET /api/v1/database/<pk>/table_metadata/extra/?name=<injection>&schema=<schema-user-can-access>
  --request args--> Table(name, schema) --raise_for_access(schema_access match) passes-->
  PrestoEngineSpec.get_extra_table_metadata --> get_create_view(database, schema, table)
  --f-string--> "SHOW CREATE VIEW {schema}.{table}" --cls.execute(cursor, sql)--> raw SQL on Presto connection
```

The `table_extra_metadata` handler loads `name`/`schema`/`catalog` from `request.args` via `QualifiedTableSchema` (string validation only) and calls `raise_for_access(database=database, table=table)`. In `SecurityManager.raise_for_access`, the `database and table` branch returns access as granted if `can_access_database` is true, or if the caller has `schema_access` on the supplied `schema` (the per-table dataset match is skipped because `force_dataset_match` defaults to False on this path). The attacker-controlled `table` string is then passed unquoted into `get_create_view`, which interpolates it into `SHOW CREATE VIEW {schema}.{table}` and executes it on the raw connection. `get_create_view` is called unconditionally by `get_extra_table_metadata`, so it is always reached. Real-world impact is constrained: Presto/Trino DBAPI does not permit stacking multiple statements in one `execute`, and `SHOW CREATE VIEW` does not accept sub-selects or `UNION`, so an attacker cannot straightforwardly turn this into arbitrary data exfiltration. The higher-impact `_partition_query` `SELECT ... $partitions` path is only reached when `get_indexes(table)` returns indexes, and `get_indexes` uses the SQLAlchemy inspector (which quotes/parameterizes the literal name), so an injection payload as the table name resolves to no such table and the partition query is not built. The residual issue is therefore an unquoted-identifier injection with limited demonstrated escalation, filed for defense-in-depth and for aggregation with any sibling sink that could make the injected name reach an executable statement.

- Target database is a Presto or Trino connection (this engine spec).
- Attacker holds a Superset account with `schema_access` on at least one schema of that database (or broader `database_access`) but not the `sql_lab` capability — i.e. they are entitled to browse metadata for that schema but not to run arbitrary SQL. This is the `schema_access` / `database_access` row of the SECURITY.md capability matrix; the escalation target is the `sql_lab` (arbitrary SQL execution) capability.
